boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's capitulation of Dornbirn (14 November 1805) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1805 group: the surrender of FML Baron Jellachich's corps in the Vorarlberg to Marshal Augereau's corps. The draft covers the French advance from Bregenz on 13 and 14 November, the skirmishes with the Austrian outposts near Bregenz and at Dornbirn, and the capitulation agreed at the French headquarters at Dornbirn while the Austrian corps stood in the Hohenems position. Jellachich's orders and movements before 13 November, the departure of his cavalry for Bohemia and its march there, and Augereau's march from the Rhine are context. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) 16 battalions and 4 squadrons, 15,000 men, under Marshal Augereau, and side B (Austrian) 9 battalions, 4,000 men, under FML Baron Jellachich. By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Moriggl's order of battle at the Rhine crossing gives Augereau's corps 16 battalions, 4 squadrons and 14,907 men (claim moriggl-order-of-battle): Bodart's battalions and squadrons equal the table's and his 15,000 is its total rounded up, but the passages read do not show that he took his figures from such a table or that the whole corps was at hand at Dornbirn. Moriggl's narrative gives no total for side A and quotes a report from side B of an enemy corps of about 9000 men (claim wolfskehl-report); Victoires gives none. Bodart's side B figure is not in the passages read: Moriggl gives the corps that capitulated as 3 generals, 160 officers and 3895 men (claim moriggl-side-b), 4,058 together (our sum, not a source's total), and the passages read do not show Bodart's basis or whether his 4,000 counts the cavalry that had left before the capitulation. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the entry: 'the French (16 battalions, 4 squadrons = 15,000 men) under Marshal Augereau force the Austrians (9 battalions = 4,000 men) under FML Baron von Jellachich to capitulate, by which the Austrians were allowed, against the obligation not to serve against France for one year, to withdraw freely to Bohemia'.

claims.value: Side B (Austrian), the Austrian account's figures: Moriggl gives the Austrian corps that capitulated as 3 generals, 160 officers and 3895 men. Jellachich had had 13 squadrons under his command; early on 13 November the colonels Kinsky and Wartensleben left Bregenz without his permission with 10 squadrons of their regiments (Klenau Chevauxlegers and Blankenstein Hussars) and 6 guns, and in the night of 13 to 14 November 2 squadrons of Rosenberg Chevauxlegers followed, so that a single squadron remained to him. The regiment Beaulieu, on the march to Landeck, had already joined Prince Rohan's corps by the time the capitulation was to cover it.
claims.rationale: Side B's own side's figures (Moriggl writes the Austrian and Tyrolean account), read from the page images. The count is of the corps as it capitulated, after the cavalry had gone; Moriggl names no source for it and gives no number of men for the departed squadrons. The corps was in the Vorarlberg before the engagement, and the cavalry left by the colonels' own decision, not the commander's, so the claim is tagged inherited. In Moriggl's OCR Jellachich had written to the Archduke that he would send battalions of Beaulieu, the combined battalion and the combined cuirassier squadron to Landeck; the passages read do not say which of these left. English renderings (ours): 'General Mathieu finally agreed that the Austrian corps, consisting of 3 generals, 160 officers and 3895 men, might withdraw to Bohemia after first laying down its arms'; 'without the permission of the commander-in-chief, whom they judged quite rightly, the two colonels, as we already know, left Bregenz early on the morning of 13 November with 10 squadrons of their regiments (Klenau Chevauxlegers and Blankenstein Hussars) and with 6 guns'; 'during the night of the 13th to the 14th 2 squadrons of Rosenberg Chevauxlegers followed as well, so that of the 13 squadrons the commander had under his orders only a single squadron remained to him'; 'by article 5 the capitulation of Dornbirn was also to apply to the regiment Beaulieu, on the march to Landeck, if on 14 November at 7 in the evening it had not joined Rohan, or was on the Arlberg'; 'the union of the said regiment with the prince's corps had, however, already taken place by this time'; 'he would at once send all dispensable baggage, ... (OCR) battalions of Beaulieu, the combined battalion and the combined cuirassier squadron to Landeck' (OCR).

claims.value: Side A (French) in Moriggl: on 13 November the brigade of the French General Serazin entered Bregenz at 4 in the afternoon and the second brigade, Sarut, at 6 in the evening, so that the whole division Mathieu was in Bregenz, followed toward midnight by another detachment. At 11 in the forenoon on 14 November the French division Desjardins, of the brigades Lapisse and Lamarque, entered Bregenz and followed the other troops, which had already marched off toward Hohenems; some detachments had taken the direction of Staufen, others the Bregenzerwald. Marshal Augereau, commandant of the VII Army Corps, arrived at Bregenz at noon coming by way of Lindau, and the General of Artillery Dorfner by way of Wangen at almost the same time. Moriggl's narrative gives no strength for side A.
claims.rationale: Side B's account of side A, read from the page images; Moriggl names no source for it. He does not name the troops that attacked the outposts on 13 November; Mathieu's division entered Bregenz that evening and Desjardins's division came up on 14 November. The passages read do not say on whose orders, and Augereau himself arrived at Bregenz only at noon on the 14th, so the phase is unresolved. The passages do not say whether the detachments sent toward Staufen and the Bregenzerwald were of Desjardins's division or of the troops ahead of it. Moriggl's order of battle at the Rhine crossing is recorded in claim moriggl-order-of-battle. Moriggl prints the marshal's name 'Augernau'. English renderings (ours): 'at 4 o'clock in the afternoon, in consequence of the convention concluded, the brigade of the French General Serazin entered Bregenz and was quartered on the citizens'; 'at 6 o'clock in the evening the second brigade, Sarut, came in, so that on the evening of the 13th the whole division Mathieu was already in Bregenz, followed toward midnight by yet another detachment'; 'on 14 November at 11 o'clock in the forenoon the French division Desjardins, consisting of the brigades Lapisse and Lamarque, entered Bregenz with Turkish music, but did not stop in the town, following at once on the heels of the other troops, which had already marched off toward Hohenems'; 'some detachments of them had taken the direction of Staufen, others had gone off toward the Bregenzerwald, evidently intending to turn the position of the imperial troops at Hohenems and bring them between two fires'; 'at noon, at 12 o'clock, the commandant of the VII Army Corps, Marshal Augereau, arrived at Bregenz coming by way of Lindau, and by way of Wangen at almost the same time the General of Artillery Dorfner'.

claims.value: Side A was Marshal Augereau's corps, the VII Army Corps in Moriggl. In Victoires, Napoleon had entrusted Augereau with a corps formed of troops that had been posted on the coasts at Brest (OCR); Augereau crossed the Rhine, passed the defiles of the Black Forest, advanced on Lake Constance, forced the Austrians to abandon Lindau and Bregenz and marched toward Feldkirch; General of Division Maurice Mathieu and General-Major Wolfskehl, authorized by their generals-in-chief, settled the articles of the convention. In Moriggl, on 13 November the enemy attacked and pushed back the imperial outposts near Bregenz, and an armistice for the town was agreed on condition that the French could occupy it at once; that evening Wolfskehl brought Jellachich a proposal of the French General of Division Maurice Mathieu to grant the whole Austrian corps free withdrawal with its arms and 8 guns in return for the evacuation of the Vorarlberg, on condition that it bound itself not to serve against France or her allies for half a year. On 14 November the French threw the Austrian outposts at Dornbirn out of the village and over the Dornbirner Ach; Wolfskehl had the firing stopped there and awaited Mathieu; at the French headquarters at Dornbirn the French demanded unconditional surrender, and General Mathieu finally agreed that the corps could withdraw to Bohemia after laying down its arms.
claims.rationale: Side A's decisions as the accounts give them (page images except where marked OCR). The passages read do not show Augereau's own orders at Bregenz or Dornbirn: Moriggl has him arrive at Bregenz at noon on the 14th and has Mathieu make the offer and agree the terms (claim moriggl-side-a). Victoires prints Wolfskehl's name 'Woffskell'. English renderings (ours): 'Napoleon had entrusted to Marshal Augereau the command of a corps formed of the troops that, at the time of the declaration of war with Austria, were posted on the coasts at Brest' (OCR); 'Augereau crossed the river on the bridge of boats that had earlier been set up to secure the communication of the department of the Haut-Rhin with the Breisgau, passed the defiles of the Black Forest, advanced on Lake Constance, forced the Austrians to abandon Lindau and Bregenz'; as in claim victoires-side-b for the march toward Feldkirch; 'General of Division Maurice Mathieu and General-Major Wolfskehl, authorized by their generals-in-chief, settled the articles of this convention, by which the Austrian corps, prisoner of war on parole, obtained leave to withdraw to Bohemia after laying down its arms'; Moriggl, as in claim side-b-command for Jellachich's journey to Bregenz on 13 November and as in claim side-b-information for the skirmishing he heard there; 'soon afterwards the reports came in that the enemy was attacking the imperial outposts and pushing them back'; 'this came about on condition that the French should be allowed to occupy the town at once'; 'Wolfskehl arrived late in the evening at Hohenems and brought the news of the entry of the said French detachments'; 'at the same time also a proposal of the French General of Division Maurice Mathieu: "to grant the whole Austrian corps free withdrawal with muskets and side arms and 8 guns in return for the evacuation of the Vorarlberg, on condition that it bind itself not to serve against France or her allies for half a year"'; 'but the advantages of the French had already grown so much that they demanded unconditional surrender'; as in claim moriggl-side-b for Mathieu's agreement.

claims.value: FML Baron Jellachich commanded side B. In Moriggl's OCR he had answered the Archduke's order to draw in his posts in Swabia and follow with his corps to Landeck with representations for being allowed to stay where he stood, and a later letter of his contained no word of beginning a retreat. On 5 November at Hohenems he ordered part of his troops back toward the Arlberg, then, informed of the French entry into Innsbruck and the Archduke's retreat, stopped the movement and ordered the retreat into the position of Hohenems, where entrenchments were now built. On 11 November, after Rohan's letter reached him at Stuben, he hastened on to Landeck and found the prince already on the march toward Bozen; their conference agreed that Rohan would continue toward Bozen and the troops from the Vorarlberg follow him without delay, but a chain of misunderstandings, which Moriggl passes over, prevented it. Back at Feldkirch on the 12th, he told Wolfskehl in the night to the 13th that he meant to defend the Vorarlberg after the example of 1799 and 1800, and the news that the colonels Kinsky and Wartensleben had left with the cavalry did not change his resolve. On 13 November, having ordered the troops' disposition at Hohenems, he went with Wolfskehl to Bregenz, made the necessary arrangements as the outposts were pushed back, and, not meaning to hold Bregenz but to bring his troops in good order into the Hohenems position, had Wolfskehl negotiate an armistice for the town until six in the evening, and so brought his men back unpursued. Mathieu's offer of that evening was not taken up. On 14 November, as the French came on, he called a council of war, in which, allegedly, all present but he voted for an honourable capitulation, until he too consented; he gave Wolfskehl full powers, and on news that Rohan had left Landeck hurried himself to the French headquarters at Dornbirn to obtain a favourable capitulation before the enemy learned of it. He was later tried by a court martial and acquitted. In Victoires the Austrian general, soon surrounded and cut off from the Tyrol, decided to ask for a capitulation on the best possible terms.

claims.value: Bodart records that on 14 November the French under Marshal Augereau forced the Austrians under FML Baron Jellachich to capitulate, the Austrians being allowed to withdraw freely to Bohemia against the obligation not to serve against France for one year. In Moriggl the Austrian corps was allowed to withdraw to Bohemia after first laying down its arms; under the convention the men were not to serve against France for a year and the officers kept their horses and baggage; the men were escorted in several columns through Bavaria to Bohemia and handed over there to the Austrian outposts from 4 to 7 December. By its article 5 the capitulation was also to apply to the regiment Beaulieu, then on the march to Landeck, if at 7 in the evening of 14 November it had not joined Rohan, or was on the Arlberg; it had by then already joined the prince's corps. In Victoires the Austrian corps, prisoner of war on parole, obtained leave to withdraw to Bohemia after laying down its arms.

claims.value: Bodart places Dornbirn, a market town in the Vorarlberg, 10 km south of Bregenz. In Moriggl, Jellachich's position was at Hohenems, where entrenchments were built, a strong position that could, however, easily be turned on the right side; on 13 November the Austrian outposts fell back over the Ach bridge and formed behind Lauterach, and on the 14th those posted at Dornbirn were thrown out of the village and over the Dornbirner Ach; French detachments took the direction of Staufen and the Bregenzerwald, in Moriggl's reading to turn the Hohenems position. claims.value: Side B's task was set from above and changed. In Moriggl's OCR the Archduke ordered Jellachich to draw in his posts in Swabia, move the stores to Landeck and follow with his corps; then, in a precise order, to lead the rest of his troops by Immenstadt to Reutte, where Prince Rohan was awaiting him; after Scharnitz was summoned, to try to reach Innsbruck by Reutte with the greater part of his troops; and then wrote that he would probably not find the road through the Vintschgau free either, solely because he had not followed the orders so often received, and that it would now be most expedient for him to take position in the Vorarlberg and at the same time occupy the Arlberg. At Stuben on 11 November Rohan passed on the Archduke's order to march off by forced marches to Bozen without regard to the arrival of the troops from the Vorarlberg, and Jellachich's conference with Rohan agreed that those troops should follow Rohan without delay; FML Hiller awaited them at Bozen.

claims.value: In Moriggl, side B's main body stood in the position of Hohenems, into which Jellachich ordered the retreat on 5 November and where entrenchments were then built; Moriggl writes that Jellachich seems to have counted too much on this strong position, which could, however, easily be turned on the right side. His outposts were thrown out of the village of Dornbirn.
claims.rationale: Code B_fortified because a cited passage names entrenchments at the position side B held when it capitulated. The passages read describe no assault on them: French detachments moved to turn the position and the corps capitulated. No works are named where the outposts fought, near Bregenz and in the village of Dornbirn. The phase is left unresolved: the passages say entrenchments were built after Jellachich ordered the retreat into the position on 5 November, not on whose order or that they were built for this engagement. Side A fought from no works. English renderings (ours): as in claim side-b-command for the retreat into the Hohenems position, the strong position and the return of his men to it; as in claim moriggl-side-a for the turning detachments; as in claim side-a-command for the outposts at Dornbirn.

open_questions: Deferred: Moriggl's OCR text before p. 434, read in full in the selection and cited only where marked OCR (Jellachich's position in Swabia after Ulm, his reconnaissance there, his reports to the Archduke and the Archduke's orders); his quotation of a military writer on obedience (p. 437, OCR), not cited; the text of the convention, of which Moriggl quotes only article 5; any report of Augereau or Mathieu, the bulletins of the Grande Armée and the record of Jellachich's court martial, none of which the passages read cite; and Victoires's account of Ney's corps closing the Tyrol to Jellachich (p. 218, OCR), not cited because p. 219 says the same from the page image; the rest of Moriggl's order of battle (pp. 89-94: the other corps, the cavalry reserve, the Guard, the recapitulation, which repeats the VII Corps' total, and the troops that arrived later), read from the page images except p. 91, read in the OCR, and not cited; and Moriggl's other name for the event: a footnote on p. 394, the summary of the chapter that begins on p. 396 and the table of contents (OCR) call it the capitulation of Hohenems, while his footnote on p. 437 calls it the capitulation of Dornbirn, read and not cited since no claim turns on the name. Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated in values: the dates of the Archduke's orders, of Jellachich's reports, of his stays at Feldkirch and of the courier's return; the number of Beaulieu battalions Jellachich proposed to send to Landeck; the regiment and squadrons the Archduke ordered to Innsbruck; the page numbers of the parent, read from the OCR except where a page image is cited.

Most consequential gap: side A's strength at Dornbirn. The targeted follow-up, Moriggl's order of battle of the Grande Armée at its crossing of the Rhine (pp. 89, 92 and 93, transcribed from the page images), gives Augereau's corps 16 battalions, 4 squadrons and 14,907 men, which Bodart's 16 battalions, 4 squadrons and 15,000 men match (claim moriggl-order-of-battle). That narrows the gap without closing it: the table is the corps at the crossing, Moriggl's narrative names only the divisions of Mathieu and Desjardins at Bregenz and quotes Wolfskehl's report of about 9000 men, and Victoires gives no figure. A return of Augereau's corps for mid-November or a report of Augereau or Mathieu, none of which the passages read cite, could close it. The detachment that escaped is uncertain too: Victoires gives about three thousand five hundred men, fifteen hundred of them cavalry; Moriggl gives 12 squadrons and 6 guns but no number of men.

Disputes recorded in the claims: side A's strength (Bodart 15,000, matching the 14,907 of Moriggl's order of battle at the Rhine crossing; Wolfskehl's report about 9000); the detachment that escaped (Victoires about three thousand five hundred men under General Wartensleben, fifteen hundred of them cavalry; Moriggl 12 of the 13 squadrons and 6 guns under the colonels Kinsky and Wartensleben); where side B's main body stood (Victoires Feldkirch, Moriggl Hohenems); the terms (Bodart free withdrawal to Bohemia against a year's service; Moriggl withdrawal after laying down arms, a year's service, the officers keeping horses and baggage; Victoires prisoners of war on parole after laying down their arms); the works (Moriggl names entrenchments at Hohenems, Victoires none). Side B's strength agrees closely: Bodart 9 battalions, 4,000 men; Moriggl 3 generals, 160 officers and 3895 men.

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his side A strength matches Moriggl's order of battle at the Rhine crossing, though the passages read do not show whether he drew on it or on a common source, his side B strength is not in the passages read, and his one year matches Moriggl's); Moriggl (the Austrian and Tyrolean account of 1861, an interested one; for the Vorarlberg and for his order of battle he names no source in the passages read, and he quotes Wolfskehl's report, Hiller's notice, Rohan's letter, the agreement at Landeck, Mathieu's offer and article 5 of the capitulation, none inspected as originals); Victoires et conquêtes (the French compilation of 1819, an interested one, which names no sources in the passages read and may draw on the bulletins, not checked).
